court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: A hotel employee was convicted of keeping a disorderly house/house of assignation based on two policemen registering with women and being shown to bedrooms; the Appellate Division reversed, holding the evidence insufficient because there was no proof the hotel was a disorderly place, frequented by vicious people, or the site of unlawful doings.

quotes.text: The evidence was insufficient to prove that the hotel was a disorderly house, or house of assignation. There was no evidence that it was a disorderly place, or frequented by disorderly or vicious people, or of any unlawful doings in it.

It is an indictable offense at common law for the keeper of an inn or hotel to refuse to receive any guest and entertain him with meals or lodging or both, and our Penal Code (section 381) makes it a misdemeanor to do so, “without just cause or excuse.”
What was done by the police against this hotel could probably be repeated in the case of most if not all of our hotels, fashionable or plain, high or low.

notes: Borderline: this is a criminal disorderly-house/vice prosecution against a licensed hotel rather than a lodging-house licensing case, but the court affirms the innkeeper's ordinary duty/right to receive and lodge paying guests and requires real proof of misconduct before treating a hotel's letting of rooms as unlawful, so flagged favorable to lawful short-term letting for pay.
